options.text: `claude import [source]` starts an interactive session that runs `/import` to bring configuration from other coding agents into Claude Code, and accepts the same `--dry-run` and `--yes` options as the command — so the dry run is the right first step for a team that wants to review before committing. Two availability caveats: it is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry or Claude Platform on AWS, and it is unavailable when you turn off feature-flag fetching.
`claude import` is a headless conversion that rewrites another agent's configuration into Claude Code's formats and exits. `--dry-run` prints the resulting CLAUDE.md without opening a session.
There is no import mechanism. Migration is manual: copy the other agent's rules file to the repository root as `CLAUDE.md` and recreate each command as a file in `.claude/commands/`.
`/import` copies configuration from a Claude Code session into another coding agent. The direction is the reverse of what the platform team assumed.

questions.explanation: There is a first-class migration path and it is interactive by design. `claude import [source]` starts an interactive session that runs `/import` to bring configuration from other coding agents into Claude Code, and it accepts the same `--dry-run` and `--yes` options as the command — so a team that wants to see the shape of the conversion before committing anything has a documented first step rather than a guess. The availability caveats matter for a fleet rollout because they are not universal: the command is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry or Claude Platform on AWS, and it is unavailable when you turn off feature-flag fetching. Vireo Labs' manual alternative is coherent as a fallback, but it loses the review step, and it is worth remembering what the destination formats actually accept — CLAUDE.md is standing context, while a procedure belongs in a skill, and a command file cannot use the `name` or `paths` frontmatter fields.

whyWrong.B: It describes a non-interactive converter that does not exist. `claude import` opens an interactive session running `/import`, and there is no headless rewrite-and-exit form.
whyWrong.C: It denies the mechanism. Import exists, and the manual copy it describes also loses the distinction between standing instructions and on-demand procedures, which is the part that decides where each piece belongs.
whyWrong.D: It reverses the direction. `/import` brings configuration into Claude Code from other coding agents, not out of Claude Code into another tool.

questions.mindset: `claude import` / `/import` migrates other agents' configuration into Claude Code — interactive, with `--dry-run` first, and unavailable on some model platforms.

questions.scenario: Meridian's CI bootstrap script needs to confirm how a runner is authenticating and which configuration directory it is using, before it decides whether to export a key or ask a human to sign in. The script wants machine-readable output.
questions.stem: What is the documented command, and what does its output actually contain?

options.text: `claude auth status` shows authentication status as JSON, with `--text` for human-readable output, exiting 0 when logged in and 1 when not. The JSON includes a `configDirectory` field naming the configuration directory the CLI uses — that field requires Claude Code v2.1.268 or later — and its `authMethod` field is one of `none`, `claude.ai`, `oauth_token`, `api_key`, `api_key_helper` or `third_party`. That is the information a bootstrap needs: `api_key_helper` and `third_party` in particular tell the script a credential is being supplied from outside the environment.
`claude auth status --json` prints the account email, the organisation id and the workspace id, so the bootstrap can select the right billing workspace without an extra API call.
`claude doctor` reports the authenticated account and the configuration directory as part of its read-only diagnostics, which is why the bootstrap should shell out to that instead.
There is no non-interactive way to inspect authentication. The bootstrap must attempt a trivial API call and infer the credential from whether it succeeds.

questions.explanation: `claude auth status` is the documented non-interactive inspection point. It shows authentication status as JSON, with `--text` for human-readable output, and exits with code 0 if logged in and 1 if not. Two fields are directly useful to a bootstrap: `configDirectory` names the configuration directory the CLI uses — which is the field that tells a script whether it is about to read the settings it thinks it is, and it requires Claude Code v2.1.268 or later — and `authMethod` is one of `none`, `claude.ai`, `oauth_token`, `api_key`, `api_key_helper` or `third_party`. The `authMethod` values matter because they distinguish the cases a bootstrap handles differently: an `api_key` is in the environment, an `api_key_helper` is a script the CLI calls, and `third_party` is a different vendor's credential entirely. JSON output is already the default, so there is no `--json` flag to add; and `claude doctor` is the read-only diagnostics command for installation and settings health rather than for credential identity.

whyWrong.B: It invents a flag and a richer payload than the command provides. The JSON status carries the `configDirectory` and `authMethod` fields described, not account and workspace identifiers.
whyWrong.C: It reassigns the command's purpose. `claude doctor` covers install health, settings-file validation errors and Remote Control eligibility; authentication identity is what `claude auth status` reports.
whyWrong.D: It denies a documented interface. The command exists precisely so a script can inspect credential state without making an API call.

questions.mindset: `claude auth status` prints JSON with exit codes 0/1; read `authMethod` and `configDirectory` before deciding how a runner authenticates.

questions.scenario: Meridian's CI review job behaves unlike every developer's session: some project-scoped servers load without the approval dialog an engineer sees, prompts it cannot answer are denied, and a personal skill the reviewer relies on does not exist for the job at all.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about making the headless configuration deliberate are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Two of the three differences are prompt-related and have documented flags. Claude Code prompts for project-scoped MCP servers in interactive sessions, while in `claude -p` runs, Agent SDK sessions and cloud sessions it cannot show the prompt and so loads them without asking — to keep one out, block it with `disabledMcpjsonServers`, exclude project settings with `--setting-sources`, or run with `--strict-mcp-config`. And where nobody can answer, `--permission-prompts none` makes Claude Code deny rather than leave a prompt outstanding, which is the honest setting for an unattended run.

The third difference is not a prompt at all — it is which sources load. Personal skills live in `~/.claude/skills/` on the engineer's machine, and neither Cowork nor cloud sessions read that directory, while cloud sessions additionally load project skills committed to the cloned repository's `.claude/skills/`. So a skill that only exists on one developer's laptop is simply absent from the job, and the fix is either committing it to the repository or enabling it for the account — not anything to do with approval dialogs. Which files load is controlled with `--setting-sources`, whose list is inherited by sessions started from this one.

All three differences reduce to the same cause: the job runs with fewer settings sources. MCP approval, prompt handling and skill visibility are all symptoms of `--setting-sources` being narrowed, so widening the list to `user,project,local` resolves all three.

None of this is a real difference. Claude Code presents an identical configuration to interactive and headless sessions; the job's behaviour differs only because it authenticates with an API key instead of signing in to claude.ai.

questions.explanation: The useful move is to stop treating headless as 'interactive minus the dialogs' and enumerate the differences, because each has a flag or a documented behaviour. On MCP: Claude Code prompts for project-scoped servers in interactive sessions, and in `claude -p` runs, Agent SDK sessions and cloud sessions it cannot show the prompt, so it loads them without asking — which is why the job sees a server the engineer had to approve. To keep it out, block it with `disabledMcpjsonServers`, exclude project settings with `--setting-sources`, or run with `--strict-mcp-config`. On permissions: with `--permission-prompts host` the default, prompts go to the Agent SDK host or a `--permission-prompt-tool`; with `none`, nobody can answer and Claude Code denies. On skills and settings generally: personal skills under `~/.claude/skills/` are not read by Cowork or cloud sessions, while cloud sessions do load project skills committed to the repository's `.claude/skills/` — so the missing skill is a source problem, and `--setting-sources` is the lever that decides which settings files load.

whyWrong.C: It collapses three independent mechanisms into one. Narrowing `--setting-sources` changes which settings files load; it does not restore an interactive MCP approval dialog, nor change who answers permission prompts — those are separate from the skill-visibility question.
whyWrong.D: It denies the documented differences and substitutes an unrelated variable. Authentication method affects whether account skills sync; it is not what makes a project-scoped server load without approval in a headless run.

questions.mindset: Headless is not interactive minus dialogs: MCP approval, unanswerable prompts and personal-skill visibility each have a different documented mechanism.
